articles.title: Bild lança empreendimento de studios e hotelaria em Londrina | G1
articles.standfirst: Na zona sul, o novo projeto da Bild reúne moradia, locação e lazer com curadoria exclusiva. Pré-lançamento em setembro.
articles.summary: Na zona sul, o novo projeto da Bild reúne moradia, locação e lazer com curadoria exclusiva. Pré-lançamento em setembro.
articles.body:
Londrina (PR) — Enquanto os studios se consolidam como um dos formatos mais procurados do mercado imobiliário londrinense, o Grupo Bild chega ao segmento na cidade com algo que poucos podem apresentar: mais de dez anos desenvolvendo e acompanhando a gestão de empreendimentos de studios e hotelaria em outras praças do país. É esse repertório que dá origem ao Ello Studios, segundo empreendimento da construtora em Londrina, com pré-lançamento previsto para setembro.

O Ello traz uma arquitetura arrojada em uma torre única, com studios de 28 m² a 65 m², estruturado desde a convenção de condomínio para acomodar tanto quem vai morar quanto quem vai locar por curta ou longa temporada — ou alternar entre essas possibilidades conforme o momento de vida. No térreo, um boulevard com lojas mantém o endereço em movimento do dia à noite.

No encontro de três vias arteriais da zona sul

O terreno ocupa o encontro das avenidas Adhemar de Barros, Harry Prochet e Waldemar Spranger, três vias arteriais de trânsito fluido na zona sul da cidade. Na prática, isso significa saída rápida para o aeroporto e para a rodovia, e acesso direto à Gleba Palhano, ao centro, ao lago Igapó, aos shoppings Catuaí e Aurora, além de universidades e hospitais.

Para o morador, é a conveniência de resolver o dia sem depender de trajetos longos. Para quem pretende explorar a locação por temporada, a proximidade do aeroporto e da rodovia é o que sustenta a demanda de quem chega à cidade a trabalho ou de passagem.

A região da Nova Prochet é uma das que mais se valorizam em Londrina, impulsionada por empreendimentos que atraem comércio, serviços e novos investimentos. Foi ali que a Bild lançou o Oase, há doze meses, cujas obras já estão em andamento.

O lazer do Ello foi pensado para quem usa o espaço de formas diferentes ao longo do dia. Bem-estar e convívio funcionam como elos do mesmo desenho: as áreas comuns se conectam e se misturam, sem fronteira entre uma vocação e outra.

No eixo de bem-estar estão o sky fitness, o spa com sauna seca, a piscina, o espaço yoga e a área wellness. No de convívio, coworking, meeting room, sala de podcast, cokitchen, pool gourmet e pool bar junto à piscina, além de pub grill e wine bar no rooftop.

São mais de 18 itens de lazer e serviço, todos entregues equipados, climatizados e decorados. A divisão entre bem-estar e convívio responde a uma pergunta prática: o que serve a quem fica três dias e o que serve a quem fica três anos. Boa parte do conjunto atende aos dois, e é isso que sustenta a versatilidade do empreendimento.

"Um studio precisa de um olhar para a área de lazer como extensão dele. Trabalhamos para que metragem eficiente não signifique abrir mão de conforto, estrutura ou identidade, e o desenho das áreas comuns é onde isso fica mais evidente"

Gabriela Yanagui, gerente comercial da Bild em Londrina

Uma década de studios e hotelaria no portfólio

O Grupo Bild está presente no mercado imobiliário há 19 anos, com mais de 105 empreendimentos lançados e mais de 70 já entregues, e é reconhecido como a 11ª maior construtora do país no ranking INTEC 2026. No portfólio de studios e hotelaria, três empreendimentos entregues e em operação com bandeiras nacionais e internacionais: o CIVITAS, em Ribeirão Preto (2015, complexo multiuso, operação Mercure, Ibis e atual Transamérica); o INTERCITY, em Bauru (2018, hotel com operação Intercity); e o HUB, também em Ribeirão Preto (2019, hotel Intercity e studios para curta e longa temporada).

"Um produto como esse não se resolve na planta, se resolve na operação. E operação se aprende entregando e acompanhando empreendimentos ao longo de anos. É essa década de expertise em studios e hotelaria que trazemos para o mercado de Londrina, que respeitamos e ajudamos a desenvolver."

Eric Dourado Jorge, sócio-diretor do Grupo Bild

No 8º andar, o sky fitness leva a assinatura da Cimerian, marca nascida em Londrina e presente em academias de referência no país, com equipamentos brasileiros de performance mundial.

Já as unidades privativas contarão com opções de entrega turn key, equipada e decorada, prontas para morar ou alugar, com a curadoria da Vessen, empresa por trás de grandes marcas hoteleiras e de resorts nacionais e internacionais. Nas áreas comuns, amenidades completam o conjunto como lavanderia, bicicletários, estacionamento e infraestrutura para carregamento de carro elétrico.

É assim que a Bild define o Ello Studios. O pré-lançamento acontece em setembro. Interessados podem conhecer o empreendimento no showroom da construtora, na Avenida Adhemar Pereira de Barros, 765. A entrega está prevista para agosto de 2030.

articles.title: Zuenir Ventura: corpo do jornalista é velado na ABL | G1
articles.standfirst: Jornalista morreu aos 95 anos nesta terça-feira (22). Durante mais de 60 anos de atuação, Zuenir construiu uma obra marcada pela cobertura de episódios políticos e temas sociais relevantes do país.
articles.summary: O corpo do jornalista Zuenir Ventura é velado nesta quarta-feira na ABL, após uma trajetória de 60 anos marcada por coberturas políticas e sociais.
articles.body:
O corpo do jornalista Zuenir Ventura é velado na manhã desta quarta-feira (23) na Academia Brasileira de Letras (ABL), da qual era imortal.

Zuenir morreu aos 95 anos nesta terça-feira (22) , no Rio de Janeiro . Durante mais de 60 anos de atuação no jornalismo, construiu uma obra marcada pela cobertura de episódios políticos e temas sociais relevantes do país.

Pouco depois das 10h, o corpo chegou ao local, acompanhado pela família. Antes da entrada da imprensa, os parentes tiveram um momento reservado de despedida.

Mestre Zu deixou a mulher, Mary Ventura, e 2 filhos, o jornalista Mauro Ventura e a editora Elisa Ventura.

O enterro está previsto para esta tarde, no mausoléu da ABL no Cemitério São João Batista, em Botafogo.

Mary Ventura ao lado do caixão com o corpo do marido, Zuenir Ventura, na ABL — Foto: Jéssica Evelin Araújo/g1

A jornalista Miriam Leitão destacou o legado de Zuenir e sua importância para o jornalismo e para o Brasil.

“Ele era gentil, generoso, muito inteligente e bem-humorado. É uma perda para o jornalismo, mas também uma grande perda para o Brasil. Ao mesmo tempo, fiquemos com tudo o que o Zuenir nos ensinou. É um legado que não termina”, afirmou.

Amigos prestaram homenagens. Coroas de flores foram enviadas pelo presidente Lula, pelo prefeito Eduardo Cavaliere, pelos colegas de redação do jornal O Globo e pelos editores da Companhia das Letras.

articles.title: Governo Netanyahu chama críticos de 'papagaios' e acusa ONU de 'viés sistemático' contra Israel; VÍDEO | G1
articles.standfirst: Premiê israelense discursará na Assembleia Geral da ONU na quinta (24). Governo israelense publicou vídeo feito com IA e site para expor o que chamou de 'mentiras' de agências da ONU contra o país durante a guerra em Gaza.
articles.summary: Premiê israelense discursará na Assembleia Geral da ONU na quinta (24). Governo israelense publicou vídeo feito com IA e site para expor o que chamou de 'mentiras' de agências da ONU contra o país durante a guerra em Gaza.
articles.body:
Às vésperas do discurso do premiê na Assembleia Geral da ONU , o governo Netanyahu chamou os críticos de Israel de "papagaios" e acusou o órgão multilateral de adotar um "viés sistemático" contra Israel.

Em resposta a líderes de Estado que já criticaram Israel na Assembleia Geral da ONU deste ano e como ação preventiva aos desafetos que ainda vão subir ao púlpito, o governo Netanyahu divulgou um vídeo feito com IA de papagaios no plenário da assembleia repetindo "culpe Israel" (leia mais abaixo) .

Além disso, o governo israelense também divulgou um site para expor o que chamou de "mentiras" e "viés sistemático" das agências da ONU contra o país durante a guerra em Gaza —travada entre Israel e o grupo terrorista Hamas entre 2023 e 2025 e que destruiu o território palestino e deixou mais de 70 mil mortos.

No site, o governo Netanyahu acusou agentes da ONU de "manipular informações com um viés abrangente e sistemático" durante o conflito , afirmou que o órgão internacional fabricou acusações de genocídio em Gaza e negou que haja fome generalizada no território palestino. Também relembrou o escândalo envolvendo a relação de funcionários da UNRWA com o Hamas .

Propaganda de Israel chamando críticos de 'papagaios' (à esquerda) e site acusando agências da ONU de adotar 'viés sistemático' contra o país durante a guerra em Gaza. — Foto: Divulgação/governo de Israel

As acusações contra Israel de realizar genocídio e de causar um cenário de fome generalizada em Gaza foram feitas, respectivamente, por uma comissão especialista contratada pela ONU composta por juristas e investigadores e pelo IPC, maior autoridade alimentar do mundo e ligada ao órgão internacional. Israel nega as acusações.

Entre os líderes que teceram críticas a Israel durante seus discursos na Assembleia Geral na terça-feira estão o presidente Lula, o presidente da França, Emmanuel Macron, o secretário-geral da ONU, António Guterres, e o rei jordaniano Abdullah II.

Lula voltou a dizer que Israel praticou genocídio em Gaza. O governo Netanyahu não havia respondido até o momento;

Macron criticou as situações humanitárias em Gaza e na Cisjordânia. O governo Netanyahu chamou as declarações de "grotescas e estarrecedoras";

Guterres disse que a escala das mortes em Gaza não se compara a nada que ele viu em seu tempo à frente da ONU. Israel o acusou de perseguição;

Abdullah pediu o respeito da lei internacional na Cisjordânia. Israel respondeu dizendo que o rei jordaniano não tem autoridade para falar sobre o tema.

Netanyahu afirmou que em seu discurso na Assembleia Geral da ONU na quinta (24) ele vai "dizer a verdade" sobre as tropas israelenses e sobre o prefeito de Nova York, Zohran Mamdani, a quem acusou de apoiar o Hamas e incitar ódio contra judeus residentes da cidade norte-americana. Ele não deu mais detalhes, porém seus discursos costumam ser marcantes.

O premiê viajará nas próximas horas aos EUA. Mamdani tentou viabilizar nos últimos meses a prisão de Netanyahu quando ele viesse a Nova York para cumprir um mandado emitido pelo Tribunal Penal Internacional (TPI) por crimes de guerra. Apesar de ter sido contrariado pelo governo Trump, Mamdani voltou a chamar o líder israelense de "criminoso de guerra".

Primeiro-ministro de Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu, e prefeito de Nova York, Zohran Mamdani. — Foto: Ronen Zvulun/Reuters/Arquivo/Andres Kudacki/AP

articles.title: Homem morre após ser perseguido e baleado, em Pinda | G1
articles.standfirst: Crime aconteceu na noite desta terça-feira (22), no distrito de Moreira César.
articles.summary: Crime aconteceu na noite desta terça-feira (22), no distrito de Moreira César.
articles.body:
2º DP Delegacia Pindamonhangaba. — Foto: Reprodução/Street View

Um homem de 34 anos morreu após ser baleado na noite desta terça-feira (22), no distrito de Moreira César, em Pindamonhangaba .

De acordo com a apuração, o crime aconteceu por volta das 22h20, na Rua Maria Augusta da Silva Pouza.

Os policiais estavam realizando um patrulhamento quando avistaram dois suspeitos correndo pela rua. Ao serem abordados, um dos rapazes admitiu ter participado de um homicídio.

No local do crime, a vítima estava com quatro lesões causadas por disparos de arma de fogo. Ela foi socorrida por outras pessoas e levada à UPA de Moreira César, onde não resistiu e morreu.

Com os suspeitos, os policiais encontraram uma arma de fogo e pelo menos 54 munições intactas. A arma foi apreendida.

Um dos suspeitos foi preso em flagrante, enquanto o outro, menor de idade, foi apreendido pela Polícia.

O crime foi registrado como homicídio no 2º DP de Pindamonhangaba e segue em investigação.

articles.title: 'A maior dor que senti': viúva homenageia Bruno Avelar após acidente | G1
articles.standfirst: Nas redes sociais, Lívia Avelar relembrou momentos vividos com o empresário e afirmou que será difícil conviver com a ausência do marido.
articles.summary: Nas redes sociais, Lívia Avelar relembrou momentos vividos com o empresário e afirmou que será difícil conviver com a ausência do marido.
articles.body:
A jornalista Lívia Avelar usou as redes sociais para homenagear o marido, o empresário mineiro Bruno Avelar , que morreu aos 41 anos na queda de um helicóptero em Santa Catarina.

Em uma publicação acompanhada por fotos do casal, Lívia lamentou a perda e afirmou estar vivendo "a maior dor" da vida. "Ainda não consigo entender, explicar ou pensar que já não terei você aqui ao lado", escreveu ( veja postagem mais abaixo ).

Na mensagem, com mais de 100 mil curtidas e dois mil comentários , a jornalista relembrou momentos vividos ao lado do marido e destacou o aprendizado compartilhado durante a relação.

"Você foi o meu maior presente e mesmo em pouco tempo nós vivemos os melhores dias das nossas vidas", escreveu Lívia.

Bruno Avelar era empresário, investidor, palestrante e fundador do projeto "O Poder do Network". Natural de Belo Horizonte, ele deixa dois filhos. O casal havia se casado há pouco mais de um mês.

O empresário estava entre as cinco vítimas do helicóptero que desapareceu na segunda-feira (21) durante um voo entre Porto Belo e São Joaquim, em Santa Catarina. Os destroços da aeronave foram encontrados na terça-feira (22), na região de Urubici.

Postagem feita por Lívia Avelar, casada com Bruno Avelar, morto em acidente com helicóptero em Santa Catarina. — Foto: Redes sociais

articles.title: AI malware is becoming its own category: Researchers found a malicious program that uses multiple AI models to decide what to do
articles.summary: Tech News News: Researchers have reportedly found a malicious program that uses AI model to help decide what it should do next. The malware, called CLOSEDQUORUM, can .
articles.body: Researchers have reportedly found a malicious program that uses AI model to help decide what it should do next. The malware, called CLOSEDQUORUM, can contact up to four AI models, including DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral and Google Gemini. Instead of relying only on instructions written by its developers, the program asks these AI systems for guidance and uses their responses to decide its next steps. Reported by Wired, the discovery was made by researchers at Cisco Talos, who have also created an open-source framework to track malware that uses AI.How does the AI-powered malware workCLOSEDQUORUM is designed for Windows and can use several AI services at the same time. Researchers describe the setup as a kind of “hive mind”, because the malware can seek decisions from multiple AI models. If one AI service is unavailable, the others can continue working.As stated in the report, researchers also found no mechanism that would allow a human to step in and control the process.The malware is designed to steal login credentials and cryptocurrency. Researchers also found links to cybercrime forums discussing credit-card fraud dating back to 2025. However, they could not confirm who created CLOSEDQUORUM or whether it has been used in real-world attacks.Researchers are finding more AI-powered malwareCisco Talos created the Cognitive Artifact Intelligence Research Network (CAIRN) after researchers began finding signs that attackers were integrating AI into malware. Ryan Fetterman of Cisco Talos said AI integration leaves behind identifiable “fingerprints” that can help researchers track and classify these programs.“The core idea is that AI integration has these vestiges, like fingerprints, that are left behind... That gives us a signal that we can use to track these samples, classify them, and look at what's happening,” Fetterman said.When Fetterman first searched for AI-integrated malware, he found only around nine named malware families, along with several proof-of-concept examples. After CAIRN was developed, researchers identified about 20 additional examples within a few months.What the findings suggestThe findings suggest that AI is becoming more deeply integrated into some malware rather than simply being used by hackers to write code or create phishing messages. Matt Olney of Cisco Talos said attackers are now beginning to operationalise AI.“Initially, everyone saw AI as a productivity tool, right?... Now what we're seeing is that it's becoming operationalized.”He said AI could allow attackers to run more campaigns, target more systems and handle different computers because the technology can provide responses and guidance in the background.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2025, a father and his 18-year-old son pushed a rowboat from San Francisco to Hawaii; nearly seven weeks and 2,400 miles later, they made history
articles.summary: US News: In a historic journey, Tim and Harrison Crockett made waves by becoming the first father-son pair to row from San Francisco to Hawaii, raising awareness for veterans' mental health along the way. Discover their harrowing yet inspiring 47-day voyage across nearly 2,400 miles of open ocean.
articles.body: One of the most solitary sports in the world, ocean rowing requires participants to spend weeks by themselves on open water with nothing but oars and willpower. Few people ever do it, and even fewer decide to tell their family about the experience. An American father and his son completely altered the equation in the summer of 2025 when they set out from California to demonstrate that they could cross the Pacific Ocean together.The trip was launched by former member of Britain's Royal Marines Commandos and Special Boat Service, Tim Crockett, and his son Harrison, then 18. They set out from San Francisco Bay on 3 June 2025 in a 24-foot rowboat they christened The Kraken. Their destination was Hilo Bay on the Big Island of Hawaii, a crossing of almost 2,400 nautical miles of the Pacific, known by rowers as the Mid Pacific route. The campaign, called Tame the Kraken, had a purpose that went well beyond the physical challenge itself.A voyage beyond lossCrockett’s link to ocean rowing was not sport, but sadness. Years before, a close buddy and fellow Special Forces man had taken his own life after dealing with the symptoms of post-traumatic stress. The death inspired Crockett to find a way to raise awareness for veterans’ mental health, and in 2018 he rowed solo across the Atlantic Ocean to achieve just that. The Pacific crossing with Harrison was meant to be a continuation of that effort, to promote a programme called Row to Recovery, which uses rowing as a kind of treatment for veterans suffering from impairments, PTSD and traumatic brain injuries.That aim affected how father and son undertook the voyage. They rowed in shifts, one always resting while the other pulled the oars. They faced weeks of relentless physical strain. They battled swells, exhaustion and rain that soaked their gear for days at a stretch. There were early moments when the enormity of the project nearly overwhelmed Harrison, he later said, remembering a moment when he just wanted to walk away. But their training and discipline through the expedition kept them going, oar stroke after oar stroke, over open ocean with no backup vessel behind.The physical demands were matched by extended spells of isolation, punctuated by occasional moments the duo would remember for the rest of their lives. One evening, as the sun was setting over the water, Harrison later recounted seeing a pod of dolphins swimming alongside the boat, calling it one of the most beautiful sensations of the voyage. There was a bit of a break from the monotony of rowing at least 12 hours a day in a boat that had no toilet and hardly enough room to sleep.Setting a record on arrivalTim and Harrison Crockett rowed into Hilo Bay on July 20, 2025 after 47 days, 14 hours and 53 minutes at sea to become the first father and son pair to complete the Mid Pacific journey unaided. Crowds gathered at a hotel near the waterfront to welcome them, and the emotional reunion with Crockett's wife and daughter marked the end of a voyage that had pushed both men to their limits. Such ocean rowing records are recorded and certified by the Ocean Rowing Society International, the organisation that has been the official advisor on human-powered ocean crossings for many years, and the Crocketts have attempted to get their achievement recognised through that procedure.Their accomplishment also makes Harrison one of the youngest persons ever to finish a trans-Pacific row, a record that adds a new chapter to a sport better known for solitary veteran adventurers than for teenagers. For Tim, who had already demonstrated he could cross an ocean alone in 2018, rowing this trip with his kid brought an altogether new level of pressure, one based around safeguarding someone he loved rather than simply surviving hardship on his own.Past the finish lineThe end of the row was never the end of the narrative. The money donated during the voyage will assist in kickstarting Row to Recovery as a comprehensive recreational treatment programme centred in Atlanta, providing veterans with an organised outlet to use rowing as a physical activity and a contemplative focus. Tim Crockett said he thinks the repeated motion of rowing helps people stay completely present, which he says could help veterans manage the anxiety and hypervigilance that typically come with PTSD.Achievements of this scale are normally scrutinised by bodies like Guinness World Records, which works with ocean rowing authorities to validate new milestones after the paperwork and tracking information have been checked. That formal acknowledgement may or may not come. But the Crocketts have already done something unusual, turning a personal mission born of grief into a physical feat that took nearly seven weeks, thousands of miles and enormous trust between a father and his son to pull off.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2012, a man in Australia used Google Earth to retrace Indian rail lines from childhood; 25 years after vanishing, he found his mother
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Stories of family separation seldom have happy endings, and searches for missing family members that are carried out decades after the incident typica.
articles.body: Stories of family separation seldom have happy endings, and searches for missing family members that are carried out decades after the incident typically come to a standstill due to faded memory and missing documents. However, in 2012, an Australian businessman managed to overcome these challenges by using only fragments of his upbringing and a satellite mapping program to find the precise Indian village from which he had been removed as a five-year-old. This quest resulted in a 25-year reunion with his birth mother.Saroo Brierley, formerly Sheru Munshi Khan, grew up in an impoverished family in central India. He would tag along behind his older brother Guddu on odd jobs around the local train stations. In 1986, the two boys pulled into a station, hunting for loose coin, and Saroo fell asleep waiting on a deserted, motionless train, while his brother went looking elsewhere. When he woke, the train was moving, carrying him alone across roughly 1,500 kilometres of unfamiliar countryside to Calcutta, a city he had never seen and could not name.Surviving alone on the streetsSaroo lived on the streets of Calcutta for weeks at a time, sleeping under station seats and dodging people who wished him ill. Eventually a teenager took him to the local police, and he was put in a government centre for lost children before being transferred into the care of an orphanage. That’s where Mrs Saroj Sood, founder of the Indian Society for Sponsorship and Adoption, attempted and failed to identify his family with the bits of information he could give as a little child who couldn’t name his hometown precisely. Saroo was officially registered as a lost child and put up for international adoption after authorities were unable to locate his family.Saroo was adopted by an Australian couple, John and Sue Brierley, who lived in Hobart, Tasmania, in 1987. He was brought up in a nurturing environment, with a second adopted son from India coming along later, and in most ways fashioned a stable, successful existence away from the land of his origin. But his early childhood memories never completely faded, remaining with him in fragments of streets, a fountain and the sound of trains rumbling by his old home.Satellite photos turned into cluesAs an adult, Brierley began to search Google Earth, scanning the panorama of India from above, hoping that pieces of recollection would finally match something on the screen. He determined how far he reasonably could have gone by rail in about 14 hours and created a search radius out from Calcutta on the map, spending countless hours looking over satellite images of locations within that range. Brierley systematically narrowed his search with the mapping tool's built-in ruler, tracing railway lines and canals that matched fragments of memory from his childhood.The breakthrough occurred when an internet landscape element matched a waterfall he remembered playing near as a youngster. This took him down a line of visible train tracks until a town called Khandwa came onto the screen. A name he didn't know, but when he zoomed in, the streets looked eerily familiar. He pointed to a fountain beside the tracks where he recalled playing and worked out a route through the street around it to what appeared to be his childhood house.A reunion 26 years onConvinced he had found his hometown, Brierley flew to Khandwa in early 2012 and started asking people whether they knew of a family that had lost a little boy decades before. Local people quickly directed him to a woman who lived nearby, and within moments he was face-to-face with his birth mother, Kamla, who had taken the name Fatima in the years since his absence. She never ceased believing her son could still be alive.But their reunion came with tragic news. Not long after Saroo’s disappearance, Guddu, the sibling Saroo had been waiting for on the day he disappeared, had died on the train tracks, a loss his mother had borne silently for 25 years. Brierley later wrote a memoir, A Long Way Home, about the entire odyssey; it was made into an Academy Award nominated film, Lion, drawing worldwide attention to a narrative that began with nothing more than a satellite map and a five-year-old’s broken memory of home.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In California, Fort Ord trained about 1.5 million soldiers; its former Army grounds now hold 86 miles of trails, wildflowers and mountain lions
articles.summary: US News: Along California's Central Coast, large tracts of unspoiled coastal land are becoming less common as decades of urbanisation gradually fill in the ope.
articles.body: Along California's Central Coast, large tracts of unspoiled coastal land are becoming less common as decades of urbanisation gradually fill in the open space between towns and highways. One noteworthy exception is located just outside of Monterey, where a former military facility that trained over a million soldiers has remained mostly intact due to decades of restricted military use that unintentionally preserved one of the last great wild landscapes in the area.Fort Ord was created by the US Army in 1917 as a field artillery training location along Monterey Bay and eventually became one of the largest Army installations on the West Coast. It served as an important staging area for forces headed to the Pacific during the next several decades, training soldiers prior to World War II, the Korean War and the Vietnam War. During its active years, Fort Ord was one of the largest training grounds in the country’s military history, with 1.5 million American troops passing through it, according to numbers supplied by the Bureau of Land Management.Land formed by restricted accessIronically, the heavy military use protected most of the surrounding terrain from the kind of commercial growth that transformed other parts of the Monterey Peninsula. For much of a century the landscape remained closed to farming, housing and roadbuilding because huge portions of Fort Ord were live fire training zones and artillery ranges, allowing native grasslands, oak woods and marine chaparral to continue mostly undisturbed. When the facility finally shut down in 1994 under a government realignment scheme following the end of the Cold War, most of that area was left in a condition rarely seen elsewhere along the more populated California coast.Recognising the ecological and historic significance of what remained, President Barack Obama signed a proclamation in April 2012 designating about 14,651 acres of the former base as Fort Ord National Monument. The proclamation, signed under the authority of the Antiquities Act, permanently protected the property, citing both its unique ecological diversity and its significance to generations of American military service.A landscape for wildlifeToday the monument spans open meadows, dense stands of chaparral and oak woodland, connected by more than 86 miles of routes for walkers, bicyclists and equestrians. The terrain supports an extraordinary diversity of wildlife for a site so close to a major metropolitan area. Bobcats, coyotes, badgers, and mountain lions live in the area, along with rare and protected species such as the California tiger salamander and the Smith’s blue butterfly, one of the first insects in the country to be given a dedicated conservation reserve. Wildflowers dot the grasslands with the changing seasons, from the bright goldfields of spring to purple nightshade later in the year, attracting hikers and naturalists throughout the year.Managed by the Bureau of Land Management, the monument also has tangible vestiges of its military heritage, such as clearly designated and gated-off explosive ordnance areas, a relic of decades of service as an active training range. Visitors are requested to stay on authorised pathways to conserve vulnerable habitat and to avoid hazards still hidden in some portions of the landscape that have not yet been entirely removed.An old battleground turned public sanctuaryMore than three decades after the last soldiers trained there, Fort Ord has become a silent counterpart to its own history, a site once marked by artillery fire and marching columns now defined by birdsong, wildflowers and the sounds of mountain bikes on packed dirt trails. The BLM is continuing to improve public access and trail infrastructure at the site, creating milestones that tie the monument’s military history to its present-day role as protected public property. The government said the site’s dual heritage will be part of a broader celebration of American service in 2026, when the very same ground on which soldiers prepared for war is now welcoming hikers, bikers and families experiencing one of California’s last vast expanses of open coastal wilderness.For a landscape that was closed to the public for much of the twentieth century, and shaped by the necessities of the military, the transformation of Fort Ord into a protected national monument is an unusual example of how sometimes it is not active conservation efforts that save a landscape, but the fact that it is inaccessible, allowing it to be saved long enough for permanent protection to catch up with it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A kidney wait since 2024 ends with an Army airlift and a rare double transplant
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: An 18-year-old who had spent nearly two years waiting for a kidney, undergoing dialysis twice a week and with no family donor, received not.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An 18-year-old who had spent nearly two years waiting for a kidney, undergoing dialysis twice a week and with no family donor, received not one but two kidneys from a single brain-dead donor on Monday — after the organs were airlifted from Chandimandir to Delhi. Both kidneys were transplanted into Anil Yadav at Safdarjung Hospital, and he is doing well.The donor, 62-year-old Amar Chand, father of an Air Warrior, had undergone coronary artery bypass graft surgery last year and was on dual antiplatelet medication. He later slipped in his bathroom, suffered a head injury and brain haemorrhage, and was declared brain dead at Command Hospital (Western Command), Chandimandir. His organ donation helped save other lives. His liver was transported to Army Hospital (Research & Referral), Delhi, for transplantation, while both corneas were donated to Command Hospital, Chandimandir.His family’s decision to donate his organs set off a race against time. With Army support, the two kidneys were airlifted to Delhi and taken to Safdarjung Hospital, where doctors transplanted both into Anil, who has chronic renal failure.“This is the first en bloc renal transplant at the hospital, in which both kidneys from a donor with marginal renal function were implanted in a single recipient. With a severe shortage of organs nationwide, accepting marginal kidneys can help expand the donor pool and give more dialysis patients, many of whom wait for years, a chance at transplantation,” said Dr Himanshu, Professor & Academic Head, Department of Nephrology, VMMC & Safdarjung Hospital. “The patient is recovering well, with good renal function and urine output.”“The most difficult part of organ donation is counselling a grieving family to say yes within two hours,” said Col Anurag Garg, Transplant Coordinator and Palliative Physician at CHWC. “I have seen this in the Subedar’s family, a Colonel’s wife’s family and Air Warrior Ranbir’s case.”Anil had been waiting for a transplant since 2024, with no donor available in his family. Until Tuesday, twice-weekly haemodialysis had been part of his routine.For a teenager who had spent nearly two years waiting for a donor, the journey from a brain-dead donor in Chandimandir to a transplant table in Delhi took place in time to give him a chance at life beyond dialysis.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A 1950 Washington bridge carrying about 90,000 vehicles a day is getting a $114 million overhaul; engineers will replace its movable span with a fixed one floated into place during a single 56-hour closure
articles.summary: US News: A bridge that has carried Washington traffic for more than seven decades is headed for a major transformation, but commuters may barely notice the mos.
articles.body: A bridge that has carried Washington traffic for more than seven decades is headed for a major transformation, but commuters may barely notice the most dramatic part of the work. The nearly half-mile-long Northbound I-395 bridge over the Potomac River is set for a $114 million rehabilitation that will replace its movable span with a new fixed structure during one tightly scheduled 56-hour weekend closure, states an online report by Field News. The construction is expected to begin next year, with completion planned for fall 2029, adds the report.A major rebuild for a 1950 bridgeAccording to Field News, Skanska USA Civil will lead the design-build project for the District Department of Transportation, working with AECOM and Genesis Structures on the design team. The project is jointly funded by DDOT and the Federal Highway Administration. Built in 1950, the four-lane bridge carries roughly 90,000 vehicles every day and forms part of a five-structure crossing connecting Arlington, Virginia, with Washington, D.C., adds the report.The rehabilitation will go well beyond repairing an aging roadway. One of its central elements is the replacement of the existing 175-foot, double-leaf bascule span, the movable section that allows river traffic to pass.New span floated into positionAs per the report, engineers will use accelerated bridge construction methods to limit disruption to one of the region's busiest transportation corridors. Instead of constructing the replacement span entirely in place, the new fixed section will be assembled beside the existing bridge. It will then be floated into position during a single 56-hour weekend closure, the report explains.Also, the compressed installation window is expected to require specialised marine equipment, rigging and carefully coordinated construction crews. The project will also replace the vessel protection system around the bascule piers and upgrade bridge barriers to meet modern collision standards. Approach spans will undergo superstructure and substructure rehabilitation, while overhead sign structures, lighting and drainage systems affected by construction will also be replaced, adds the report.Heavy construction activity through 2029The bridge sits beside Skanska's separate Long Bridge North project, a roughly $1 billion effort being delivered with FlatironDragados to expand rail capacity through the same Arlington-Washington corridor. With both projects progressing in the same area, the river crossing zone is expected to remain a significant centre of heavy civil construction through the end of the decade.For contractors and subcontractors, the I-395 rehabilitation is expected to create opportunities across several specialised areas, including marine work, structural steel, traffic control, signage, lighting, drainage and bridge-barrier upgrades. The most unusual phase will be the float-in operation, where decades of bridge history will give way to a new fixed span in less than three days.Image Courtesy: ARL NowCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2023, Philadelphia lawyer Andrew Coval left legal work for $16.14-an-hour seasonal ranger work, sharing a FEMA trailer while working in Yosemite
articles.summary: US News: In 2023, Andrew Coval made an unusual career change. The Philadelphia lawyer left his legal work behind, drove a 2000 Toyota Camry across the United S.
articles.body: In 2023, Andrew Coval made an unusual career change. The Philadelphia lawyer left his legal work behind, drove a 2000 Toyota Camry across the United States and arrived in California to work as a seasonal ranger at Yosemite National Park. The job came with a very different lifestyle: long days outdoors, shared accommodation in an old FEMA trailer and an hourly wage of $16.14. For Coval, however, the attraction was not the pay or the comfort. It was the opportunity to work inside one of America’s most recognisable national parks.A very different life in YosemiteThe San Francisco Chronicle notes that Coval said his first year was a total contrast to his previous professional career. In place of the Philadelphia office, he worked among campgrounds, roads, forests, and visitor centres. He resided in park housing in an old FEMA trailer along with two other seasonal workers. His job was equally varied. According to Coval, he was required to check campers, answer questions, address bear-related food-storage issues, put out campfires, and solve campsite-related problems. Sometimes, he had to do some rather unpleasant things as well.That wide range of responsibilities was part of what made seasonal work important at Yosemite. The National Park Service describes seasonal jobs as an important part of its workforce. The work can vary widely, from talking to visitors and maintaining park facilities to helping with resource management and law enforcement. Many of these positions are available during the summer, when more visitors arrive in the parks.For Coval, the seasonal job was also a chance to get closer to the career he had always wanted. He said in his article that he was comfortable earning $16.14 an hour because the opportunity to work as a ranger mattered more to him than the pay. The following year, he returned to Yosemite as an interpreter, leading educational programmes and answering visitors’ questions at the Big Oak Flat Visitor Centre.What seasonal rangers actually doThe job of a park ranger can be seen as just giving maps or directions to park visitors. The role involves far more than that. The people working at Yosemite have to manage a park that spans about 759,620 acres, with approximately 800 miles of trails and hundreds of facilities. The National Park Service has also documented hundreds of automobile accidents and multiple search and rescue missions every year.That workload becomes more complicated when millions of visitors arrive within a relatively short period. Yosemite’s visitor-access planning documents identify congestion, long entrance queues, pressure on facilities, human waste and insufficient staffing during periods of heavy use among the challenges created by intense visitation. Research published in Environment Systems and Decisions examined the working conditions of rangers across protected areas and found that many face hazardous environments alongside employment insecurity, inadequate income and limited workplace protections.When a dream job meets a difficult systemCoval’s experience also showed how uncertain seasonal work can become when the hiring system changes. In an account published in 2025, he wrote about thousands of seasonal employees being caught up in new federal hiring procedures, leaving some appointments in limbo. Some workers, he noted, might decide not to return, while others could find themselves waiting longer for their paperwork to be processed. It was a reminder that behind the scenery and outdoor work, seasonal jobs at national parks can also come with plenty of uncertainty.For Coval, though, the attraction of Yosemite was never difficult to explain. He had swapped the familiar path of a legal career for long days outside, shared accommodation and a much smaller pay cheque. Yet the experience gave him something his previous job could not: the chance to work in a place he had long wanted to be. His move from a Philadelphia law office to a FEMA trailer in Yosemite may sound like an unlikely career change, but for Coval, it was a way of turning an old ambition into everyday life.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2026, Big Bear’s famous eagle Jackie vanished from her nest cam; public videos helped identify her before rescuers found her injured near the lake
articles.summary: US News: For years, millions of people had watched Jackie, a bald eagle nesting near Big Bear Lake in California, on a livestream focused on her nest. In July .
articles.body: For years, millions of people had watched Jackie, a bald eagle nesting near Big Bear Lake in California, on a livestream focused on her nest. In July 2026, that familiar presence suddenly disappeared. Jackie was no longer appearing on the camera, leaving viewers wondering where the female eagle had gone. Days later, videos recorded by members of the public helped link a badly injured bald eagle found near the lake to the missing bird.According to Friends of Big Bear Valley, the organisation operating the livestream, an adult bald eagle was spotted on the ground near Big Bear Lake on July 16. The following day, witnesses recorded the bird involved in a brief confrontation with two younger eagles. Cellphone footage showed the adult defending itself with its talons but struggling to fly away. Rescuers eventually found the eagle in the water and brought it to the San Dimas Raptor Rescue team.From a livestream to a real-world searchFriends of Big Bear Valley set up their first nest cam in 2015 and later expanded the network to show a broader view of the surrounding area. The goal was to watch the wildlife without disturbing the birds and to make the nesting birds among the most closely observed in the valley. Over the years, the livestream also gave viewers a close look at the eagles that returned to the nest, making Jackie a familiar presence to a large online audience. That connection became important when an injured adult eagle was rescued, as there was initially no way to tell whether the bird was Jackie. Friends of Big Bear Valley asked people not to jump to any conclusions while the eagle was being rescued. The organisation later confirmed that the eagle was indeed Jackie.Jackie and her partner, Shadow, have nested there since 2016, according to the organisation’s history. Their nesting history included snowstorms, failed eggs, successful hatchings and chick development. In 2026, their eggs failed to hatch, adding another chapter to a story followed by a large online audience. The incident turned the livestream from a simple viewing tool into a source of valuable information. Although the nesting camera did not reveal Jackie’s location, the online community understood its importance.What rescuers foundThe eagle that had been rescued was weak and could not fly properly. Los Angeles County Parks and Recreation said the bird was stabilised before being sent to Ojai Raptor Centre for treatment. Preliminary tests did not reveal any signs of external damage, although the bird was lethargic and anaemic. Specialists believed the bird had been fighting with other eagles. The video from the mobile phone was especially valuable since it clearly showed the adult eagle defending itself from an attack. This explained why a bird that could still fly had been found on the ground and in the water.Research published in the Journal of Raptor Research provides context for encounters such as the one involving Jackie, examining the territorial behaviour and interactions of birds of prey. Bald eagles are closely associated with waterways because fish are an important part of their diet, while their nesting territories can be defended against other eagles. Jackie’s confrontation reflected the natural pressures wild eagles face, though the livestream made it unusually visible to viewers.Jackie’s final chapterAccording to the Ojai Raptor Centre and the Associated Press, Jackie received treatment for severe anaemia, including a blood transfusion and oxygen therapy. Her condition showed some improvement after the transfusion, but her health later deteriorated. She died on August 9, 2026, after more than three weeks of treatment at the centre. The news prompted an outpouring of grief from longtime viewers of the Big Bear livestream, and the California Department of Fish and Wildlife took custody of her remains.Her story also highlighted how wildlife watching has changed in the digital age. The camera, originally set up to monitor the nest, drew a large audience that became familiar enough with the birds to notice when one was missing. After Jackie disappeared from the video, viewers did not know all the facts, but photos and videos from locals helped wildlife specialists identify the bird. The livestream could not help Jackie directly, but it documented her life and helped viewers piece together sightings near the end of her story.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Want to invest in real estate without buying a house? India’s REIT market is booming
articles.summary: News News: Want a slice of the real estate market without buying a house or land?You don’t necessarily need to own a property to invest in real estate, REITs can.
articles.body: Want a slice of the real estate market without buying a house or land?You don’t necessarily need to own a property to invest in real estate, REITs can be another route that lets investors put their money into income-generating properties.Real estate investment trusts (REITs) offer investors a way to invest in such properties and earn income from them. And this investment route is gaining ground in India, with the country’s REIT market now ranking as the fourth-largest in Asia by value.India’s REIT market has grown 62% to $17.7 billion, moving ahead of Hong Kong. According to a Cushman & Wakefield report, the market was valued at $11 billion at the end of 2024.So, what exactly are REITs?A REIT is a company that owns and operates real estate to generate income. It manages portfolios of high-value properties and mortgages, leases properties and collects rent, which is then distributed among shareholders as income and dividends.REITs can allow both big and small investors to put money into large commercial real estate projects. Properties held by REITs can include data centres, infrastructure, healthcare units and apartment complexes.REITs can broadly be classified based on the type of business they undertake and how their shares are bought and sold. Equity REITs generally operate and manage income-generating commercial properties, with rent being a key source of income. Mortgage REITs, or mREITs, lend money to property owners or acquire mortgage-backed securities and earn interest.Then there are also hybrid REITs, which combine equity and mortgage REITs. Private REITs function as private placements for a selective group of investors, while publicly traded REITs have shares listed on the National Securities Exchange and are regulated by SEBI. Public non-traded REITs are registered with SEBI but are not traded on the National Stock Exchange.Why should you invest in REITs?For investors, REITs can provide exposure to a mix of properties without having to manage the underlying real estate themselves. They can also offer an avenue for income, with REITs required to distribute as much as 90% of their taxable earnings to shareholders.REITs can also form part of a long-term or retirement portfolio, offering exposure to real estate as an asset class. Their income-generating potential and connection with the real estate market can make them relevant for investors looking at longer investment horizons.Investors can buy shares in publicly listed REITs through major stock exchanges. REITs are similar to mutual funds in that they pool investments, although REITs hold real estate rather than bonds or stocks. Investors can also seek assistance from financial advisers when choosing a REIT.How can you invet in REITs?Buy REIT units through stocksInvestors can purchase REIT units directly, much like buying shares of publicly listed companies on major stock exchanges.Invest through mutual funds Investors can choose mutual funds that pool money into REIT-linked funds managed by asset management companies, offering diversification.Choose REIT-focused ETFs Exchange-traded funds (ETFs) provide an indirect way to invest in REITs while also offering portfolio diversification.Expansion in the REIT market has been driven in part by the growth of listed real estate portfolios and new listings, which have added millions of square feet of office space.India’s REIT market comprised seven REITs, including two small and medium REITs (SM REITs). Six of these together held around 178 million sq ft of listed portfolio space as of June 2026, while another 36.7 million sq ft was under construction or planned.Two recent listings have contributed substantially to the increase. Knowledge Realty Trust and Bagmane Prime Office REIT added a combined 53.7 million sq ft. Together, they accounted for around three-fourths of the total new space added to the six India REITs between June 2025 and June 2026.“India’s REIT market has reached an important inflection point, with larger listed portfolios, strong occupancies and a healthy development pipeline reinforcing its institutional depth,” Somy Thomas, executive managing director, Capital Markets, India, at Cushman & Wakefield, said.The office market has remained an important support for REITs, with occupancy staying high even as Grade A vacancy tightened. Demand from multinational occupiers and the continued expansion of Global Capability Centres (GCCs) have also supported the market.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: In 2012, an Australian man retraced childhood memories on Google Earth; then flew to India and found the mother and siblings he had been separated from as a child
articles.summary: Rest of World News: At five years old, Saroo Brierley fell asleep on a train in central India and woke up alone in an unfamiliar place. According to Google’s account of h.
articles.body: At five years old, Saroo Brierley fell asleep on a train in central India and woke up alone in an unfamiliar place. According to Google’s account of his journey, the train eventually carried him about 1,500 kilometres to Kolkata, where he spent weeks surviving on the streets before being taken to an orphanage and later adopted by an Australian couple, John and Sue Brierley, who raised him in Tasmania. For years, fragments of his childhood stayed with him. More than two decades later, those memories became the starting point for an extraordinary search using Google Earth.A five-year-old's memories become a mapSaroo had no address, telephone number or clear idea of where his family lived. What he did remember were scattered images: a railway station, a bridge, a large industrial tank, a fountain and a river flowing over a dam. He also remembered travelling by train for what seemed like a long time before he reached Kolkata.According to Saroo's account, he began using Google Earth around 2009, initially without knowing whether the idea could work. He contacted Indian friends and asked them to find out how fast trains travelled in the 1980s. Using an estimated speed of about 80 kilometres per hour and his recollection that he had travelled overnight, he calculated that the station where he had boarded the train could be roughly 960 kilometres from Kolkata.Then, he created a rough search area centred on the city of Kolkata and started to look at railway lines and towns located inside it. It took time, as he spent hours poring over satellite maps and sometimes worked into the early hours of the morning. He slowly narrowed his search by evaluating which areas spoke Hindi and discarding those that did not match his memories of the weather and terrain. In effect, he used satellite mapping to search for places he recognised rather than names he could not remember.The moment Google Earth revealed KhandwaAfter months of searching, Saroo noticed a combination of landmarks that triggered a powerful memory. He found a railway station beside a bridge and a large industrial tank, both of which resembled what he remembered from childhood. The town was Burhanpur, the place where he believed he had been separated from his older brother.He then made his way along the railway line to the next station. At the next station, he noticed a river running beside the tracks and over a dam. It looked like the place which he recalled from his childhood when the water there looked like a waterfall to him. However, Saroo needed more proof. He used Google Earth to trace the route from the dam into the centre of town.It turned out to be Khandwa, in Madhya Pradesh. After that, he continued searching via YouTube and Facebook until he came across a Facebook group for Khandwa. In 2011, he posted a question on the group seeking help to identify the area he thought he grew up in. The mention of Ganesh Talai confirmed it for Saroo. Later, Google cited Saroo's search as an example of identifying a hometown using vague memories and satellite imagery.A reunion after 25 yearsAs The Guardian reported, finding Khandwa was only the beginning. Saroo did not have any guarantees yet that his mother and siblings were even alive. On February 10, 2012, he went from Australia to India. Upon arriving in Khandwa, he remembered other aspects of his childhood life and located the neighbourhood where his family once lived. What happened next was remarkable. After asking about his family, Saroo was taken to his mother, who was now known as Fatima. She had also spent many years remembering the moment of their parting.Saroo also got to meet up with his younger sister, Shekila, and his brother, Kullu. While the encounter made him happy, it also revealed a painful chapter in his family’s history. His elder brother, Guddu, had died on the railway tracks within a month of Saroo’s disappearance. Since childhood, Saroo had wondered where he came from and what had happened to his family. He finally got an answer.He finally got an answer. Google Earth did not recognise his mother or search any database of missing children. It provided Saroo with the opportunity to look at the geography of his memories from above. Railway tracks, a dam, a bridge, and a fountain turned out to be landmarks. With patience and help from people in Khandwa, those landmarks led him back to the place he had left as a small child 25 years earlier.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Two SC Justices urge CJI to set up five-judge bench for deciding constitutional issues; why it matters
articles.summary: India News: A two-judge Supreme Court bench, comprising Justice SC Sharma and Justice Datta, has requested the Chief Justice of India to explore the possibility o.
articles.body: A two-judge Supreme Court bench, comprising Justice SC Sharma and Justice Datta, has requested the Chief Justice of India to explore the possibility of setting up a permanent five-judge Constitutional Bench to deal with questions involving interpretation of the Constitution.Why this mattersConstitutional questions currently require bench formation: Under Article 145(3), cases involving a "substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution" must be heard by at least five judges.Such benches are constituted by the Chief Justice of India as required. Currently, there are 22 five-judge matters with 175 tagged matters pending in court.A permanent bench could make the process more predictable. Instead of repeatedly constituting a five-judge bench whenever a major constitutional question arises, a standing bench could hear such matters more continuously.It could also speed up constitutional litigation. Constitution Bench cases can remain pending for long periods because judges have multiple rosters and cases. A dedicated bench could potentially create greater continuity and reduce delays.A permanent bench could also bring greater consistency as the same group of judges will be dealing regularly with constitutional questions, which could develop continuity in constitutional jurisprudence, rather than different combinations of judges being assembled for different cases.It could also increase the importance of the CJI's roster decisions. The CJI is the master of the roster and decides which judges sit on particular benches. A permanent five-judge bench would therefore be a significant change in how the court allocates its most important constitutional cases.Constitution Benches decide some of the country's most consequential questions, including the limits of Parliament's power, fundamental rights, federalism, separation of powers and challenges to constitutional amendments.The Supreme Court has used Constitution Benches extensively in recent years; for example, 16 Constitution Bench judgments were delivered during former CJI D.Y. articles.title: New York’s High Line once carried freight trains above Manhattan; now the abandoned railway is one of the city’s most visited parks
articles.summary: US News: The High Line was built to carry freight trains above Manhattan’s West Side, and was responsible for moving meat, dairy, produce and other goods witho.
articles.body: The High Line was built to carry freight trains above Manhattan’s West Side, and was responsible for moving meat, dairy, produce and other goods without sending trains through crowded city streets. Freight service began on the elevated structure in 1934 and ended in 1980, and for years afterward, the railway sat unused, with plants spreading across its tracks. Today, the structure has been converted into a 1.45-mile elevated public park.Why the trains were lifted above the streetsFreight trains travelled at street level before the elevated structure was built, where they shared roads with pedestrians, automobiles and other traffic. The elevated line changed that arrangement, and trains could now move above the streets and reach factories, warehouses and loading docks along the route. New York City later described the railway as infrastructure built in the 1930s to remove dangerous freight traffic from Manhattan’s streets while continuing to deliver milk, meat, produce and manufactured goods to businesses on the West Side.Trains had stopped using the High Line altogether by 1980, and the last train carried three carloads of frozen turkeys, according to Friends of the High Line’s historical material. The structure became an abandoned piece of elevated infrastructure with tracks, ballast and vegetation left above the streets.The railway nearly disappearedThe unused structure was eventually threatened with demolition, and in 1999, neighborhood residents Joshua David and Robert Hammond founded Friends of the High Line to campaign for its preservation and reuse as public open space. An established argument faced by the organisation was that the railway was no longer carrying freight and occupied valuable land in one of Manhattan’s most heavily developed areas. Preservation campaigners proposed turning it into a public space instead of treating the structure as obsolete infrastructure.The city and Friends of the High Line eventually pursued the park idea, and the first section opened to the public in June 2009, which ran from Gansevoort Street to West 20th Street. New York City said the first section drew more than two million visitors during its first year.The tracks became part of the parkLandscape architects James Corner Field Operations, Diller Scofidio + Renfro, and planting designer Piet Oudolf incorporated portions of the old tracks into the park and designed planting areas around them. The second section, from West 20th to West 30th Streets, opened in 2011, and the Rail Yards section, which extended from north to West 34th Street, opened in 2014. The final section of the historic structure, known as the Spur, opened in 2019, which completed the main High Line park.The abandoned railway had therefore become a public landscape in stages rather than through a single redevelopment project, and more than one-third of the original rail tracks remain incorporated into the park’s design, alongside hundreds of species of plants.Friends of the High Line reported more than four million visitors annually by the early 2010s, while its more recent materials put annual visitation at about eight million. The elevated freight railway that once served Manhattan’s industrial economy is now a public park visited by millions each year.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2010, an Irishman began running around the world; four years and roughly 50,000 km later, he finished a global route few runners had ever completed
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Tony Mangan started the Dublin Marathon on October 25, 2010, kept running, and began a journey that would take him across five continents, six deserts.
articles.body: Tony Mangan started the Dublin Marathon on October 25, 2010, kept running, and began a journey that would take him across five continents, six deserts and 41 countries before he returned to Dublin four years later. The World Runners Association records his completed route at 50,000 km over 1,461 days, and lists it as the longest circumnavigation of the Earth on foot under its records.The Dublin Marathon was only the starting pointMangan had spent years thinking about running around the world, and eventually turned the idea into what he called his “World Jog”, starting with the 2010 Dublin Marathon. He continued westward across Ireland to Dunquin, the westernmost point of the Dingle Peninsula, after completing the race.Mangan crossed North America, moved through Central and South America, continued through Australia and Asia, and eventually returned to Europe. The World Runners Association’s route record lists sections through Canada, the United States, Panama, Colombia, Argentina, New Zealand, Australia, Indonesia and Turkey before the final European leg back to Dublin. Mangan averaged roughly the equivalent of a marathon a day during the journey, and also travelled with a small running buggy called Nirvana, which carried equipment including clothing, food and camping gear.50,000 km across 41 countriesThe Irish Independent reported that he had already covered 50,000 km and crossed five continents, six deserts and 41 countries in September 2014. He had begun his return through Europe after completing the long sections across the Americas, Australasia and Asia.Mangan encountered extreme conditions along the way, including severe heat and cold, and his own account of the expedition describes dehydration in Mexico, temperatures that reached minus 30C in the United States and storms in Patagonia. He also ran across the Australian outback.The World Runners Association records that Mangan undertook the 50,000-km run for Aware, which is an Irish organisation working in the area of depression. The run therefore combined his long-standing ambition to circumnavigate the world with fundraising and public awareness.The final stretch became a race against the clockBy the time Mangan reached Europe, the expedition was already approaching its fourth year. He had accumulated tens of thousands of kilometres on the road, but the final distance still required him to keep running through Ireland before returning to the Dublin Marathon where the journey had begun.In September 2014, the Irish Independent reported that Mangan was completing the last part of his journey through Ireland after returning from abroad. He had already reached approximately 50,000 km, but continued running until the expedition formally ended with the Dublin Marathon. The final race gave the journey a fixed finishing point rather than ending somewhere along the road.On October 27, 2014, Mangan crossed the Dublin Marathon finish line in 6:08:30, completing the final stage of a journey that had started with the same race four years earlier. The Irish Independent reported that he had covered roughly 50,000 km by the time he finished.He finished where the journey beganMangan returned to Ireland in September 2014 and spent the final weeks completing a roughly 1,600-km circuit of the country. He then entered the Dublin Marathon on October 27, four years after the race that had started his world run.The Irish Independent reported that Mangan crossed the Dublin Marathon finish line in 6:08:30, and brought the journey to an end after approximately 50,000 km. The finish was not at the same point where he had first crossed the line in 2010 by accident; rather, it was deliberate, since Dublin had been both the beginning and the endpoint of the route. The World Runners Association currently lists the completed run at 50,000 km and 1,461 days and identifies Mangan as holding its longest-circumnavigation record.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: Pakistan on Wednesday blocked major highways leading to the capital, Islamabad, and deployed tens of thousands of security personnel ahead of a march planned by the Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) seeking the release of its founder and jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan."Nearly 35,000 additional police and paramilitary personnel have been stationed in and around Islamabad," Reuters quoted an interior ministry official as saying."More have been deployed in other parts of Pakistan where Khan's supporters may gather," he added.Two major highways linking Islamabad to the northwestern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, governed by PTI, have also been closed until further notice, the National Highways Authority said.Shipping containers have been placed in recent days to barricade Islamabad's government district, home to parliament, the prime minister's residence and foreign embassies.Authorities have already put hospitals in Islamabad, including the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences and Federal Government Polyclinic Hospital, on high alert until September 30.Police have also detained three of Khan's sisters and hundreds of party activists in recent days, citing the need to maintain public order.On Monday, Pakistan's interior minister, Mohsin Naqvi, warned that police had been told to respond "forcefully" if the march turned violent, adding, "It is not like they come and fire shots and you do nothing."The march is scheduled for September 27.PTI refuses to back downHowever, PTI chairman Gohar Khan declared that the march would proceed despite the blockade.Khan, 73, was ousted as prime minister by parliament in a 2022 no-confidence vote. Cases against the cricketer-turned-politician, whose arrest in 2023 sparked nationwide riots, ranged from allegations involving state gifts and inciting violent attacks on military and state installations to an accusation of an unlawful marriage. All but one of his convictions have since been suspended or overturned, with appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing.The PTI's planned march comes more than a month after the government defied a court order and refused to allow Khan to receive treatment at a private hospital, despite mounting concerns over his health.The protest also comes amid public discontent over inflation and rising fuel prices that has spread beyond Khan's core supporters.The PTI's previous large-scale protest, two years ago, ended in deadly clashes with security forces.You use AI every day.
